And: Andromeda was the princess chained to a sea cliff as a sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus, and rescued by Perseus. The hazy oval near her hip is the Andromeda Galaxy, the farthest thing most people ever see with the naked eye, about 2.5 million light-years away.
Ant: The Air Pump, one of the 18th-century constellations Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille named for scientific instruments. It is faint and sits low in the south from the Badlands.
Aps: The Bird of Paradise, a far-southern constellation charted by Dutch navigators in the 1590s. It never rises over North Dakota.
Aqr: The Water Bearer, an ancient zodiac constellation pictured pouring water from a jar. Its stars are faint, but the Sun passes through it each February and March.
Aql: The Eagle that carried Zeus's thunderbolts. Its brightest star, Altair, is one corner of the Summer Triangle and spins so fast it bulges at the equator.
Ara: The Altar, where the gods swore their oath before battling the Titans. It lies deep in the southern sky, below Scorpius.
Ari: The Ram whose golden fleece Jason and the Argonauts sought. Two thousand years ago the Sun stood here at the spring equinox, which is why the equinox point is still called the First Point of Aries.
Aur: The Charioteer, often shown holding a goat and her kids. Bright yellow Capella, the goat star, is nearly overhead on winter nights in North Dakota.
Boo: The Herdsman, following the Great Bear around the pole. Follow the arc of the Big Dipper's handle to reach Arcturus, the brightest star of spring.
Cae: The Engraving Tool, a small, dim Lacaille constellation. It barely clears the southern horizon from the northern Plains.
Cam: The Giraffe, a faint 17th-century constellation filling the empty space between Polaris and Capella. It is up all night, every night, from North Dakota.
Cnc: The Crab that pinched Hercules during his fight with the Hydra. Dim as it is, it holds the Beehive, a star cluster visible to the naked eye as a soft glow.
CVn: The Hunting Dogs, held on a leash by Bootes as they chase the Great Bear. The brighter star, Cor Caroli, was named for King Charles of England.
CMa: The Great Dog, following Orion across the winter sky. Its heart is Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, only 8.6 light-years away.
CMi: The Little Dog, marked by a single bright star, Procyon, whose name means 'before the dog' because it rises just ahead of Sirius.
Cap: The Sea Goat, half goat and half fish, one of the oldest constellations on record. It is a faint triangle low in the south on autumn evenings.
Car: The Keel of the ship Argo. Its brilliant star Canopus is the second brightest in the sky, but from North Dakota it never rises.
Cas: Queen Cassiopeia, whose boast that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs set the Perseus story in motion. Her W-shaped stars circle the pole opposite the Big Dipper and are up every night of the year.
Cen: The Centaur, usually identified as wise Chiron. It holds the nearest star system to the Sun, Alpha Centauri, though that star stays below the northern Plains horizon.
Cep: King Cepheus, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. The house-shaped figure sits near the pole and contains Delta Cephei, the star that gave its name to the Cepheid variables astronomers use to measure the universe.
Cet: The Sea Monster sent to devour Andromeda, sprawling across the autumn sky. Its star Mira, 'the Wonderful,' was the first star ever seen to fade and brighten on a regular cycle.
Cha: The Chameleon, a small far-southern constellation charted in the 1590s. Not visible from North America.
Cir: The Compasses (the drafting kind), a tiny Lacaille constellation next to Alpha Centauri. Never rises over North Dakota.
Col: The Dove, sometimes said to be the one Noah released from the Ark. It skims the southern horizon below Orion on winter nights.
Com: Berenice's Hair, named for an Egyptian queen who cut off her hair as an offering for her husband's safe return from war. The faint sprinkle of stars is really a nearby star cluster.
CrA: The Southern Crown, a small arc of stars below Sagittarius. It rides just above the horizon on summer nights from the northern Plains.
CrB: The Northern Crown, the wedding crown of Ariadne that Dionysus threw into the sky. A neat semicircle of stars between Bootes and Hercules.
Crv: The Crow, Apollo's bird, punished with eternal thirst for lying about a delayed errand. Its four-sided shape is easy to spot below Virgo in spring.
Crt: The Cup, the vessel the Crow was sent to fill. A faint bowl of stars riding on the back of Hydra.
Cru: The Southern Cross, the smallest constellation and the emblem of the southern hemisphere. It is never visible from North Dakota.
Cyg: The Swan, flying down the Milky Way with its wings spread. Its tail star, Deneb, is a supergiant thousands of light-years away and one corner of the Summer Triangle; the whole figure is also called the Northern Cross.
Del: The Dolphin that rescued the musician Arion from pirates. A compact diamond of stars just east of the Summer Triangle.
Dor: The Dolphinfish, home to the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Far too far south to be seen from North America.
Dra: The Dragon, coiling between the two Bears. Thuban, in its tail, was the pole star when the Egyptian pyramids were built.
Equ: The Little Horse, the second-smallest constellation. Four faint stars just west of the Dolphin.
Eri: The River, winding from Orion's foot far to the south. Its mouth is marked by Achernar, a bright star that never rises over the northern Plains.
For: The Furnace, a chemist's furnace in Lacaille's catalog. Faint and low in the autumn sky.
Gem: The Twins, Castor and Pollux, brothers of Helen of Troy. Their two bright stars stand side by side high in the winter sky; the Geminid meteors radiate from here each December.
Gru: The Crane, a southern constellation of the 1590s. Its brighter stars just clear the horizon from the southern United States, not from North Dakota.
Her: Hercules, shown kneeling, the strongest of heroes. The Keystone at his center holds M13, a ball of several hundred thousand stars that binoculars show as a fuzzy patch.
Hor: The Pendulum Clock, a faint southern constellation from Lacaille's catalog. Not visible from the northern Plains.
Hya: The Water Snake, the longest constellation, stretching a quarter of the way around the sky. Hercules killed the many-headed Hydra as his second labor.
Hyi: The Lesser Water Snake, a small southern constellation near the south celestial pole. Never visible from North America.
Ind: The Indian, a southern constellation charted by Dutch navigators. Never rises over North Dakota.
Lac: The Lizard, a zigzag of faint stars between Cygnus and Andromeda, added in the 1680s by Johannes Hevelius.
Leo: The Lion, the Nemean lion killed by Hercules. Its head is a backwards question mark of stars anchored by Regulus, and it rules the spring sky.
LMi: The Little Lion, a dim strip of stars between Leo and the Great Bear, added in the 1680s.
Lep: The Hare, crouching beneath the feet of Orion, hunted by his dogs. A modest figure low in the winter sky.
Lib: The Scales, the only zodiac constellation that is an object rather than a creature. Its stars were once considered the claws of Scorpius.
Lup: The Wolf, held by the Centaur. Low in the south on early-summer nights, partly below the horizon from North Dakota.
Lyn: The Lynx, so named because Hevelius said you needed the eyes of a lynx to see it. A long chain of faint stars between the Great Bear and Auriga.
Lyr: The Lyre of Orpheus, whose music could charm stones. Vega, its brilliant blue-white star, is nearly overhead on summer nights and was the pole star 14,000 years ago.
Men: The Table Mountain, named by Lacaille for the mountain above Cape Town. Deep in the southern sky.
Mic: The Microscope, a dim Lacaille constellation low in the south below Capricornus.
Mon: The Unicorn, filling the space inside the Winter Triangle between Orion, Sirius, and Procyon. Faint, but the winter Milky Way runs through it.
Mus: The Fly, a small southern constellation next to the Southern Cross. Never visible from North America.
Nor: The Carpenter's Square, a small Lacaille constellation in the southern Milky Way.
Oct: The Octant, the navigator's instrument, containing the south celestial pole. Never visible from the northern hemisphere.
Oph: The Serpent Bearer, usually identified as Asclepius, the healer. Large and prominent on summer evenings, and the Sun spends more time in it than in neighboring Scorpius.
Ori: The Hunter, the most recognizable figure in the winter sky, with three belt stars in a row. Red Betelgeuse marks a shoulder, blue Rigel a foot, and the Orion Nebula glows in the sword.
Pav: The Peacock, a southern constellation from the 1590s. Never rises over North Dakota.
Peg: The Winged Horse, born from the blood of Medusa. The Great Square of Pegasus is the landmark of the autumn sky.
Per: Perseus, the hero who slew Medusa and rescued Andromeda. He holds the 'demon star' Algol, which dims every three days, and the Perseid meteors stream from here each August.
Phe: The Phoenix, the bird reborn from its own ashes. Low in the far south on autumn nights, mostly below the horizon from the northern Plains.
Pic: The Painter's Easel, a faint Lacaille constellation near Canopus. Not visible from North Dakota.
Psc: The Fishes, tied together by a ribbon, said to be Aphrodite and her son escaping the monster Typhon. The spring equinox point now lies in Pisces.
PsA: The Southern Fish, drinking the water poured by Aquarius. Its lone bright star, Fomalhaut, is the 'autumn star' low in the south.
Pup: The Stern of the ship Argo, which carried Jason and the Argonauts. Rich in star clusters, it lies low in the winter sky below Canis Major.
Pyx: The Mariner's Compass, a small constellation Lacaille placed beside the ship Argo.
Ret: The Reticle, named for the crosshairs in a telescope eyepiece. Deep in the southern sky.
Sge: The Arrow, a small, ancient constellation flying between the Swan and the Eagle. One of the smallest constellations, but easy to find inside the Summer Triangle.
Sgr: The Archer, a centaur drawing his bow at Scorpius. The center of our galaxy lies in this direction, and the summer Milky Way is thickest here; look for the Teapot shape.
Sco: The Scorpion that killed Orion, which is why the two are never in the sky together. Its red heart is Antares, 'rival of Mars,' and its curved tail hangs low in the south on summer nights.
Scl: The Sculptor's Studio, a faint Lacaille constellation containing the south galactic pole. Low in the autumn sky.
Sct: The Shield, named by Hevelius for King John III Sobieski of Poland. Small but set in a dense, bright patch of the summer Milky Way.
Ser: The Serpent held by Ophiuchus, the only constellation split in two: Serpens Caput, the head, west of the Serpent Bearer, and Serpens Cauda, the tail, to the east.
Sex: The Sextant, Hevelius's own astronomical instrument, placed between Leo and Hydra. Very faint.
Tau: The Bull, the form Zeus took to carry off Europa. Red Aldebaran is its eye, the V-shaped Hyades its face, and the Pleiades ride on its shoulder.
Tel: The Telescope, a faint Lacaille constellation below Sagittarius. Not visible from North Dakota.
Tri: The Triangle, a small but ancient constellation between Andromeda and Aries. It holds the Triangulum Galaxy, a faint neighbor of the Milky Way.
TrA: The Southern Triangle, a bright trio of stars near Alpha Centauri. Never rises over the northern Plains.
Tuc: The Toucan, home of the Small Magellanic Cloud and the great cluster 47 Tucanae. Far southern, not visible from North America.
UMa: The Great Bear, whose seven brightest stars form the Big Dipper. The two stars at the end of the bowl point to Polaris; the bear is up every night of the year from North Dakota.
UMi: The Little Bear, or Little Dipper. Polaris, at the tip of its tail, sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole, so the whole sky appears to turn around it.
Vel: The Sails of the ship Argo, in the southern Milky Way. Mostly below the horizon from the northern Plains.
Vir: The Maiden, often identified with Demeter, goddess of the harvest, holding an ear of wheat marked by the bright star Spica. The largest zodiac constellation, prominent in spring.
Vol: The Flying Fish, a small far-southern constellation from the 1590s. Never visible from North America.
Vul: The Fox, added by Hevelius in the 1680s, inside the Summer Triangle. It holds the Coathanger, a chance line of stars that looks exactly like one in binoculars.
